Neural networks attract attention out of proportion to how often they are the right choice.
The mechanics are less mysterious than the reputation suggests: a network is a stack of
weighted sums with a bend between them, trained by the same gradient descent introduced in
[4 · How algorithms learn](../04-how-algorithms-learn/index.qmd). This section builds one in
forty lines of base R, checks its gradients against finite differences, and only then uses a
package.

They shine on data whose structure a person cannot summarise into features, such as imagery,
acoustics and waveforms, and marine science has plenty of that. For a table of environmental
covariates with a few hundred rows, they usually do not. This section shows both, and the
reason for the difference turns out to be a single property of the problem.

## Findings from this section

- A single neuron with an identity activation **is** linear regression: our network and
  `lm()` agreed to **eight decimal places**. With a logistic activation it is logistic
  regression, to four.
- **Two hidden units, seven weights, recovered a humped temperature response**, placing
  its peak at 8.7 °C against a true optimum of 9.0. One unit could not; five added nothing.
  The best straight line through that hump *rises*, reporting the wrong sign.
- Backpropagated gradients matched finite differences to about **eleven decimal places**.
  Large initial weights saturated the hidden units and shrank the first-layer gradient
  **twelvefold**, which is the vanishing gradient problem in one table.
- The usable range of learning rates spans about **twentyfold**. At 2, the loss reached
  2 × 10^12^ by step twelve and overflowed to `NaN` by step 147.
- **Unscaled inputs cost more than everything else combined.** The same network on metres
  and degrees scored 0.763 where standardised it scored 0.570, and a straight line scored
  0.680. It lost to a linear model without producing a single warning.
- A 40-unit network's validation error bottomed at **step 1,937 of 8,000** and was 4% worse
  by the end. Ten identical runs differing only in seed varied by **0.046** in validation
  MSE.
- On the survey, the mean-only baseline scores 4.402 and an oracle that knows every true
  expected count scores 3.701, so **everything any method can learn is a 0.70 window**. A
  default eight-unit network never entered it at any training-set size, and
  cross-validation tuned the network down to **one hidden unit** with the heaviest penalty
  on the grid.
- **A linear autoencoder is PCA**, exactly: same reconstruction error to four decimals, a
  canonical correlation of 1.000 with the principal components. Every random seed found the
  same plane and a different pair of axes in it.
- **Seventeen weights beat a 500-tree random forest**, AUC 0.998 against 0.926, on a
  water-mass band in temperature–salinity space. Logistic regression could not exceed 0.72
  there at any sample size.

::: {.callout-important}
The network was not short of rows. It was short of **signal**. Given the same predictors and
the noise-free expected count as its target, the eight-unit network beat linear regression
by **24%**: it had learned the true response surface, and learned it well, on a few hundred
stations. Then negative-binomial sampling noise was put back on top and that advantage
vanished and reversed. "Neural networks need a lot of data" is the wrong summary. They need
a lot of data *relative to the noise*, and on a noisy count survey that is a much higher bar
than the row count suggests.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
**What makes a network win is a property of the problem, not of the data volume.** A hidden
unit computes a weighted combination of the inputs before it bends, so it is a rotated
coordinate. So networks win when what matters is a *combination* of your variables that you
cannot name in advance: a diagonal band in T–S space, an edge in an image, a formant in a
call. If you can name the combination, add it as a column and use a simpler model. If your
predictors act more or less one at a time, a forest will beat the network and cost you an
afternoon instead of a week.
:::
